chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.citation: Chapalaghi, M et al. (2022). A step-by-step assessment of the backwashing process impact on the fouling mitigation of blended PVC/PC and nanocomposite PVC/PC/MAg membranes in a membrane bioreactor (MBR) treating pharmaceutical wastewater. CHEM ENG RES DES.
chunks.text: Water is one of the most important resources for human survival. The water demand has pronounced over the past decades due to population growth, industry development, and agricultural expansion. Although groundwater, surface water, and rainwater are conventional freshwater resources, nowadays, unconventional water resources such as wastewater are recognized as valuable resources for freshwater supply. In this regard, wastewater treatment and reuse have become viable selections for providing additional water supplies (Kim and Jang, 2006) . Membrane bioreactor (MBR) systems are one of the most promising wastewater treatment technologies growing increasingly all over the world, especially in developing countries (Wu et al., 2008) . Membrane bioreactors combine conventional activated sludge (CAS) and membrane separation technologies to produce high-quality water (Zhang et al., 2021) . MBR technology reduces plant footprint by eliminating clarifiers and conventional filters, which makes them more efficient in comparison with conventional wastewater treatment processes (Judd, 2010; Deng et al., 2015) .

chunks.text: For STPs at the Los Altos and Los Altos Hills and Stanford clusters, where the average daily wastewater flows are less than the expected average daily outdoor water use, we assume that the ratio of the design flow to the average daily wastewater flow depends upon energy recovery at the STP. For STP systems that recover energy, we assume the quantity of digestate returned to the sewer is negligible, and that solids discharges can be timed so as to prevent nuisance conditions. We also assume that the ratio of the design flow to the average daily wastewater flow is 2.0. If energy is not recovered by digestion of solids, there may be insufficient flow for flushing of solids discharged to the sewer. We therefore assume that, for this case, only half of the average daily wastewater flow is treated and that the design flow is equal to the average daily wastewater flow. For satellite treatment plants, we also assume local storage of treated water. For Los Altos and Los Altos Hills and Stanford clusters, where average daily wastewater flow is less than average outdoor water use, we assume a storage capacity of 3 days at the average daily recycled water flow.

chunks.citation: Le Hyaric, R et al. (2010). Pilot-scale anaerobic digestion of screenings from wastewater treatment plants. BIORESOURCE TECHNOL.
chunks.text: A mass of 300 kg of screenings was sampled from the municipal wastewater treatment plant of Bourg-en-Bresse (Region Rhône-   Alpes, France). The waste was made of a mix of screenings from 15-mm and 3-mm screens and was compacted in the plant. The sample was taken to the laboratory where it was homogenized and divided into 20 sub-samples of 8 kg. The procedure allowed to guarantee a good reproducibility of the sub-samples composition, which was verified analytically. The samples were stored at À18 °C. A digestate sampled from a municipal solid waste (MSW) digester was used as an inoculum, in order to have active microflora and to make easier the start-up of anaerobic process. The major characteristics of the waste and the inoculum are shown in Table 4 .

chunks.citation: Wei, CH et al. (2014). Sustainable organic loading rate and energy recovery potential of mesophilic anaerobic membrane bioreactor for municipal wastewater treatment. BIORESOURCE TECHNOL.
chunks.text: An anaerobic membrane bioreactor (AnMBR) -a hybrid of anaerobic digestion and membrane separation -may overcome the drawbacks of the conventional anaerobic activated sludge process through the excellent sludge-water separation by a microfiltration (MF) or ultrafiltration (UF) membrane. The coupling of a membrane results in high biomass (and thus high OLR and organics removal), and produces a good quality effluent that has significantly lower amount of particles and pathogens (Liao et al., 2006) . Several recent reviews on published AnMBR studies over the past two decades show that AnMBR can achieve high COD removal (more than 85%, up to 99%) with low permeate COD (less than 100 mg/L, down to below 10 mg/L) under a range of hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 3-120 h, sludge retention time (SRT) of 15 d to infinity, volumetric OLR of 0.2-5 gCOD/L/d and operating temperature of 10-37 °C for real and/or synthetic municipal wastewater treatment (Lin et al., 2013; Ozgun et al., 2013; Skouteris et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2012; Stuckey, 2012) .

chunks.citation: Guo, KH et al. (2018). Comparison of the UV/chlorine and UV/H2O2 processes in the degradation of PPCPs in simulated drinking water and wastewater: Kinetics, radical mechanism and energy requirements. WATER RES.
chunks.text: In pure water, among the investigated 28 PPCPs, the UV/H 2 O 2 process was superior to the UV/chlorine process for the removal of 12 PPCPs primarily driven by HO at neutral pH values, while the UV/chlorine process was better for the other 16 PPCPs primarily driven by the RCS. The concentration of HO was lower in the UV/ chlorine process than in the UV/H 2 O 2 process, but RCS such as Cl and ClO in UV/chlorine contributed to the degradation of PPCPs with electron-donating functional groups. ClO was important to the degradation of PPCPs possessing electron-rich groups in the UV/chlorine process. The steady-state concentration of ClO was calculated to be ~3 orders of magnitude greater than that of HO , and the reactivities of ClO with 16 PPCPs were determined to be in the range of 10 6 e10 9 M À1 s À1 . The reactivity of ClO (ln k ClO ) was linearly related to the Hammett Ss pþ constant for aromatic PPCPs.

chunks.text: For the treatment phase, the actual operational energy use was based on existing secondary treatment at the WWTP, 22 which was augmented with hypothetical typical tertiary treatment processes to achieve adequate water quality for NPR. Additional treatment processes included coagulation and flocculation with appropriate alum doses 35 using rapid sand filtration and chlorination, which were each modeled independently (Figure 2 ). It was assumed that tertiary treatment was constructed at the equivalent scale of the existing plant (241 000 m 3 /day) and that it was not necessary to size for peak flows, as they would receive only secondary treatment water and not be recycled. For the decentralized facilities, it is also appropriate to design based on average flows because the equalization tank at the beginning of the treatment train is sized sufficiently to buffer the daily variations in flow rate. It is not necessary to accommodate increases in flow due to storm events because infiltration and inflow do not occur in building systems. The biosolids resulting from anaerobic digestion at the centralized WWTP were assumed to be disposed in equal parts (by mass) via land application and daily cover at a landfill, with transportation requirements and landfill emissions estimated.

chunks.text: Commonly, WW in the city was treated using an activated sludge process (ASP), which includes primary, and secondary treatment. The treatment plant was designed as per the typical inflow and outflow obtained from literature (Table 1 ). The primary treatment involves screening and sedimentation, while secondary treatment includes aeration and clarifiers. Each plant had a flowrate of 56,284 m 3 /day, while the screens and storage tanks were designed to hold a peak capacity of 3× of the typical flow. The WW collected from the city was stored in the storage tanks, which was sent to treatment process (Fig. 1 ). The treatment process starts with screening, where it removes large particles present in the wastewater. Normally, screening and gritchamber was a gravity-based process and hence no energy was consumed. After screening, the wastewater enters the primary sedimentation where solid particles with higher specific gravity (ρ ≥ 2.5) settle down.

chunks.text: As shown in Fig. 5 (f) (g), the anaerobic membrane bioreactor (AnMBR) is also a research focus in recent years. This reactor integrates AD with membrane separation technology, available in various combination forms and membrane module types as shown in Fig. 5 (d) (e) . This system efficiently traps organics, SS, pathogens and sludge in the system, and also alleviates impacts of external pollutants on the PN/A system (Kong et al., 2021c; Wu et al., 2021a) . Compared to conventional AD technology, AnMBR offers distinct advantages such as the separation of HRT and sludge retention time (SRT), maintaining higher biomass (Wei et al., 2024) , which contribute to higher biogas production, higher OLR, and better effluent quality (Kong et al., 2021a) . Studies detailing AnMBR's application in wastewater treatment are summarized in Table 3 . Although AnMBR is considered suitable for treating high-strength industrial wastewater, membrane fouling represents a significant challenge.

chunks.citation: Mascia, M et al. (2012). Fixed bed reactors with three dimensional electrodes for electrochemical treatment of waters for disinfection. CHEM ENG J.
chunks.text: A three dimensional configuration was tested for applications in electrochemical treatment of water with low chloride content. Concentration profiles of chloride and chloride oxidation by-products   were experimentally obtained and modelled with a convectiondiffusion model in a two-dimensional approximation. Under conditions of Re = 5 and i = 7.5 mA cm À2 the proposed inseries configuration of the reactor allowed to obtain concentrations of active chlorine up to 20 mg dm À3 inside the reactor. Under these conditions the faradaic yield for active chlorine generation was 30%, which is a value acceptable in the treatment of low concentrate waters. The configuration with the cathode packing downstream the anode allowed reducing the residual concentration of active chlorine by 50% of the value inside the reactor under all the conditions examined. The study demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed reactor arrangement to achieve high concentration of disinfectants inside the unit and, at the same time, to control the residual concentration down to values acceptable for water supply.

chunks.text: A pilot plant using UF as tertiary treatment for water recycling and reuse (Fig. 1 ) was built-up at the Water Resource Recovery Laboratory of Palermo University (Mannina et al., 2021) . The pilot plant was designed for an influent flow rate of 20 L/h and was fed with the effluent of a predenitrification activated sludge plant treating the real wastewater collected within the University of Palermo Campus (Mannina et al., 2021) . The pilot plant consists of a membrane tank, blower (LA-45C, Nitto Kohki, Germany), filtration and backwash pumps (Qdos30 metering pumps, Watson Marlow, UK), and UF membrane module (Fig. 1 ). Hollow-fiber UF membrane (Koch separation solutions, Wilmington -USA) having 0.03 µm pore size and 1.4 m 2 total surface area was used. The filtration and backwash pumps have 30 L/min capacity. Sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) was used for membrane chemical cleaning according to the cleaning protocol provided by the manufacturer.
